units.registry.sserGrossUnitsPerKm: illustrative ONCRA net tonnes per km over 50 years = gross x 0.64 (default 20% GHG deduction and 20% buffer; 0.52 if rated Category 3). Hedges only; 0 where carbon is an unsubstantiated scenario. Field name kept for compatibility; SSER is not an ONCRA unit.
units.carbonSequestration: tCO2e per km, gross, removal in each 5-year interval (difference in stock)
units.width: strip width in metres: land taken out of production (for hedges, the hedge width is hedgeConfig.hedgeWidthM)
units.hedgeOutputs.biodiversity.hluPerKm: SSE Biodiversity Toolkit v1.0 hedgerow units per km (screening; Moderate and Good condition)
units.hedgeOutputs.biodiversity.marginBuPerKm: SSE Biodiversity Toolkit v1.0 area units per km for the grass margin (screening)

sources.carbon.hedges: hedge_carbon_model.py v2 (3 Nov 2026): Biffi et al. 2023 Sci Total Environ 892:164482 (AGB, Table 3); Black et al. 2023 Sci Total Environ 871:162073 via Biffi 2023 s4.3 (root:shoot 0.49); Biffi et al. 2022 J Environ Manage 307:114484 (SOC, Tables 3-4); Biffi et al. 2025 Agric Ecosyst Environ 382:109471; Drexler & Don 2024 Geoderma 445:116878. Replaces HedgeCarbon.xlsx (unit and derivation errors).
sources.carbon.other: Unsubstantiated v9 scenarios (Apr 2026); excluded from carbon value and net units
sources.incomeForegone: SAC Consulting / FAS, The Farm Management Handbook, Feb 2026 updates (arable, dairy, beef, sheep); x0.7 edge factor (judgement)
sources.waterValues: 4 Nov 2026 (v12): Indicative avoided pollution damage (v12): 10 ha of arable per km; 200 kg sediment and 0.7 kg P per ha per yr; retention by strip width from Stutter et al. 2021 Table 2 width-only regressions (CITED; width explains only 13-15% of variation); delivery 1.0 riparian, 0.5 cross-slope, 0.1 down-slope (JUDGEMENT). Low case: sediment GBP0.054/kg (Defra IA Defra1819 Table 22); high case: GBP0.55/kg (CREW CRW2024/04); P GBP46.61/kg (CREW). Nitrate not valued. Not cash income; site estimate needed.
sources.carbonNetFactor: ONCRA LSC Protocol v2 s2.1.6; Guidelines (Mar 2026) s5.6: 0.8 x 0.8 = 0.64 (applied in calc.js)
sources.hedgeOptions: hedge-config.js v12 (4 Nov 2026): hedge width vs strip width (EFA greening guidance 2026; GAEC 7; AECS option pages dated 15 Dec 2025; MOREhedges); SSE Biodiversity Toolkit v1.0; Van Vooren et al. 2017; Cole et al. 2020; Stutter et al. 2021. Presets HV1-HV8 agreed 4 Nov 2026.

notes: Indicative screening estimates; not financial, legal or agronomic advice.
General Cropping margin excludes potatoes and vegetables, so income forgone is likely understated.
v11 (3 Nov 2026): corrections following the independent audit of 3 Nov 2026; see docs/audit-tracker-2026-11-03.csv.
Pollination, pest regulation, thermal, windbreak and avoided-cost values are unvalidated scenarios and are excluded from totals in calc.js.

v12 (4 Nov 2026): hedges replaced by the HV1-HV8 presets and a configurator (form, species, trees, strip width, position); water values rebuilt from Stutter et al. 2021 for all records; nitrate not valued.

hedgePresets.name: Fence-line hedge
hedgePresets.summary: The narrowest option: a 2 m double-row hedge on the boundary with the GAEC 7 2 m strip on the field side.

hedgePresets.name: Hedge and margin
hedgePresets.summary: Recommended default: a 2 m double-row hedge with a 4 m grass margin on the field side, 3 m of it beyond the GAEC 2 m line.

hedgePresets.name: Wide wildlife hedge
hedgePresets.summary: A 3 m triple-row hedge with a grass margin. Add standard trees with the trees toggle.

hedgePresets.name: Hedge with trees
hedgePresets.summary: HV2 with a native standard tree every 6-10 m: the highest SSE hedgerow distinctiveness.

hedgePresets.name: Hedge and wide margin
hedgePresets.summary: A 2 m double-row hedge with an 8 m tussocky or flower-rich margin; suits the foot of a slope.

hedgePresets.name: Contour hedge
hedgePresets.summary: An in-field hedge on the contour with a grass margin on the upslope side. Triple row by default on slopes and in NVZ catchments; double row via the toggle.

hedgePresets.name: Riparian hedge and water margin
hedgePresets.summary: A double-row hedge set back from the bank behind a grass water margin. Double row only beside water, so the grass zone can trap sediment.

hedgePresets.name: Productive hedge
hedgePresets.summary: A 4.2 m triple-row hedge coppiced for biochar feedstock. The land carbon claim is provisional soil and roots only. Does not rely on AECS.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Suitable for Fife arable boundaries (Land Classes 1 to 4.2). Targeted adjacent to field drains or ditches.
registry.plantingRegime: 100% Sown. Mix: 40% Cocksfoot, 30% Timothy, 20% Creeping Red Fescue, 10% Red Clover. Density: 20-25 kg/ha. SPH: N/A.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1: Spot spray/weed-wipe. Long-term: Annual mow & bale (post-15 Aug for nesting birds). Biomass: Must be removed to export N/P.
registry.rootArchitecture: Fibrous: Hyper-dense shallow root mat (top 0-20cm) creates a physical net that binds topsoil particles.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Nesting Hub: Ground cover for Skylark. IPM: Cocksfoot tussocks provide overwintering for predatory beetles.
registry.waterImpacts: Sediment Trap: High surface roughness slows overland flow, dropping suspended solids before the watercourse.
registry.carbonAgronomicAssumptions: Carbon profile: unsubstantiated scenario carried over from v9 (Apr 2026). No reproducible derivation or source ledger exists. Earlier claims that it follows Woodland Carbon Code curves, includes a 15% deduction, or is calibrated by growth degree days could not be verified and are not relied on. Shown for comparison only; excluded from carbon value and net units pending reconstruction. Agronomic Profile: Managed height ~0.5m - 1m (Sward/Earthwork). Prevailing risk: Damaging Spring Easterlies (Haar). Zero aerodynamic windbreak value; zero shadow drag.
registry.agronomicUtility: Infrastructure Protection: Physically stops topsoil from choking field drainage networks. Keeps headlands firm.
registry.regulatoryAlignment: Possible AECS route: Water Margins in Arable Fields (page updated 15 Dec 2025): minimum 3 m on small channels, 6 m on wider channels, 12 m at still water; payment only beyond the 2 m strip already required next to watercourses (GBR 20). Eligibility is not confirmed for any site. Using a grant may affect ONCRA eligibility (Guidelines 27 Mar 2026 s4.2.1, s8.2.2): a written ONCRA ruling is needed before grants and carbon units are combined.
registry.additionality: Not assessed. ONCRA financial additionality (Guidelines s8.2.1) and regulatory additionality (s8.2.2), including the government-grant clause (s4.2.1), are unresolved for this activity and need a written ONCRA ruling. Any biodiversity or water benefit claim needs a measured baseline and verification.

interventions.bespokePlantingRegime: Double staggered row, 6 plants/m (AECS minimum), rows about 40 cm apart. 60% hawthorn plus at least 4 other native woody species, e.g. 10% blackthorn, 10% hazel, 5% holly, 5% dog rose, 5% guelder rose, 5% crab apple. Local provenance, from the NatureScot native list. It meets the AECS rule of at least three native flowering species (AECS guidance gives 60-80% hawthorn as a typical, not required, mix) and is intended to establish at least 4 woody species per 30 m. Spatial planting, survival and survey evidence are needed to confirm species richness.

Not a 50-year forecast or a demonstrated conservative range. Not counted: needs an evidenced baseline, depth, time model and margin soil stratum.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Arable and mixed field boundaries, in-field contours and burn sides; check drains, services, peat depth and breeding waders before planting.
registry.plantingRegime: Double staggered row, 6 plants/m (AECS minimum), rows about 40 cm apart. 60% hawthorn plus at least 4 other native woody species, e.g. 10% blackthorn, 10% hazel, 5% holly, 5% dog rose, 5% guelder rose, 5% crab apple. Local provenance, from the NatureScot native list. It meets the AECS rule of at least three native flowering species (AECS guidance gives 60-80% hawthorn as a typical, not required, mix) and is intended to establish at least 4 woody species per 30 m. Spatial planting, survival and survey evidence are needed to confirm species richness.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1: mulch and weed control. Year 2: cut back hard to 45-60 cm to thicken the base. Then trim 1 Dec to end Feb on a 2-3 year rotation, never the same length every year, raising the cut about 10 cm each time; managed at about 2 m wide and 2-2.5 m tall. Margin: low-productivity grass mix with at least four flowering species; no fertiliser or sprays; cut after 15 August with cuttings removed. Do not plant on peat deeper than 30 cm or in fields used by breeding waders.
registry.rootArchitecture: Two rows of fibrous hawthorn and blackthorn roots binding the topsoil, with hazel and holly rooting deeper.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Species-rich native hedgerow (SSE distinctiveness Medium (4)). Screening SSE units: 6.7-7.82 hedgerow units/km at Moderate-Good condition (5-12 years to target). Separate area-unit examples assume an entirely cereal baseline, not this parcel: 0.37 area units/km as arable margin (0.94-1.28 if accepted as neutral grassland).
registry.waterImpacts: 3 m strip: indicative retention of about 76% of sediment and 55% of total phosphorus reaching it (Stutter et al. 2021 width-only fits; soil and slope matter more). Best value where the strip lies across the flow path.
registry.carbonAgronomicAssumptions: Carbon profile: provisional lower-end literature estimate (hedge_carbon_model.py v2 / hedge-config.js). 2 m crown; 50-year gross 52.5 tCO2e/km (biomass 24.5, roots 12, soil 15.9). Grass margin soil carbon is not counted (scenario 2.8-5 tCO2e/km). Not validated; site soil measurement replaces the soil term.
registry.agronomicUtility: Hedge centre 1 m from the boundary; 1 m of grass margin on the field side.
registry.regulatoryAlignment: Possible AECS route (rates checked 3 Nov 2026; pages dated 15 Dec 2025): Planting or Replanting of Hedges (capital GBP5.40/m) with Creation of Hedgerows (GBP1.20/m/yr). Item requirements: double-staggered rows at 6 plants/m and at least three different native flowering species (AECS guidance gives 60-80% hawthorn as a typical mix, not a requirement); livestock fencing at least 1 m from the centre line. Not suitable for freely-draining soils where wet-soil Alder will fail to establish.
registry.plantingRegime: 2 Rows (staggered). Mix: 50% Alder (Alnus glutinosa), 50% Willow (Salix viminalis or Salix fragilis). Density: 3,000 SPH. Spacing: 1m x 0.6m staggered. Select Fife local provenance Alder where available. Wet-soil tolerant planting stock essential — containerised or bare-root from specialist native nursery.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1: Weed suppression around stems; no cultivation. Year 2–3: Remove dead stock and replace failures. Long-term: No routine harvesting required. Managed as a long-term nitrate interception buffer. Optional management: light coppice of willow every 7–10 years if height management required for adjacent field operations. Keep alder a minor component (10-20%): it fixes nitrogen and can add nitrate (UKFS riparian woodland guide 2024, p.19). Biomass from any willow coppice: chipped for local biomass use.
registry.rootArchitecture: Alder roots host nitrogen-fixing Frankia; fixed nitrogen can raise nitrate leaching (UKFS 2024 p.19), so alder is kept to 10-20% in nitrate-targeted strips. Willow develops extensive lateral root mats (0–40cm) with high transpiration capacity, actively pumping excess soil moisture and dissolved nitrate from the saturated root zone. Combined root system creates a persistent biological barrier intercepting subsurface nitrate leachate pathways.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Wetland Edge Habitat: Alder and Willow provide year-round riparian structure — Willow catkins are the primary early-season pollen source for bumblebees; Alder provides cone seed for siskins and redpolls; wet soil conditions support water vole, frog, newt, and aquatic invertebrate populations. Canopy shading of the adjacent watercourse helps maintain summer water temperature below critical thresholds for aquatic life.
registry.waterImpacts: Maximum Nitrate Interception: Alder root nodule N-fixation prevents net nitrate leaching from the buffer zone itself; Willow lateral roots actively pump dissolved nitrate from subsurface leachate pathways; wet soil denitrification by anaerobic bacteria in the saturated root zone converts residual nitrate to nitrogen gas. Combined mechanisms achieve near-100% nitrate interception efficiency in the riparian position (sepaMetrics nitrateRetention=100). This is the highest-performance NVZ compliance feature in the database.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Improved pasture and dairy grazing land, particularly south- and west-facing fields exposed to summer afternoon sun. Suitable for Land Classes 2–4 on loamy to clay-loam pasture soils. Priority locations: dairy units with documented summer heat stress indicators (reduced milk yield, somatic cell count increases, reduced conception rates in July–August).
registry.plantingRegime: Open-grown single or double row. Mix: 40% Sycamore (Acer pseudoplatanus), 40% Pedunculate Oak (Quercus robur), 20% Hornbeam (Carpinus betulus). Density: 1 tree per 5–6m. SPH: ~350–400. Wide spacing essential to maximise individual crown development and ground-level light penetration to maintain pasture productivity beneath canopy.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1–5: Vole guards, tree stakes, and spot weed suppression around base. Year 3–7: Formative pruning to develop high crown (clear stem to 2–2.5m) ensuring unimpeded airflow and livestock access to shade without bark damage. Long-term: Annual inspection for storm damage; remove epicormic growth from lower stem. Biomass: Timber asset managed under long-term schedule; no routine harvest. Root-blading optional at Year 10+ if pasture productivity under canopy requires renovation.
registry.rootArchitecture: Deep Taproots: Oak develops a primary taproot to 1.5m+ depth in well-structured soils, bypassing the shallow grass root zone and drawing deep groundwater via hydraulic redistribution during summer drought. Sycamore develops a heart-root system to 80–100cm. Hornbeam lateral roots provide mid-depth pasture stabilisation. Combined deep root architecture maximises hydraulic lift to maintain adjacent pasture soil moisture during the critical July–August drought period in the East Neuk.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Thermogenesis Corridor: Mature oak canopy supports 280+ associated invertebrate species — the highest of any native tree. Hollow trunks and dead wood in mature trees provide bat roost opportunities. Open-grown sycamore provides significant aphid resource for insectivorous birds. Connects isolated pasture habitats for barn owls, bats, and avian predators hunting rodents in the field margin.
registry.waterImpacts: Drought Buffering: Deep taproot hydraulic redistribution maintains pasture soil moisture during summer drought, reducing crop and pasture stress (see droughtResilience score=80). Canopy cooling (3.75°C below ambient on hot days; Burschel & Huss 1997) reduces evapotranspiration from the shaded zone and reduces livestock heat stress. Shade also reduces soil moisture loss through surface evaporation in the shade zone.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Long, unbroken sloping arable fields (Land Classes 2–4) with overland surface runoff and rill erosion risk. Contour swales are most effective on slopes of 2–8° where laser-graded earthworks can direct and detain flow. Priority: fields with documented gully formation, compacted headlands, or watercourse siltation downstream.
registry.plantingRegime: Zoned earthworks planting. Bund (upper edge, 2m width): 100% SRC Alder (Alnus glutinosa) and Willow (Salix viminalis mix) at 10,000 SPH for immediate root stabilisation of the constructed bund. Swale (6m detention zone): sown wet-meadow grass mix — Meadowsweet, Flote-grass, Yorkshire Fog, Red Fescue — to maximise roughness and FIO trapping. Bund plants: 1-year whip, bare-root. Swale seed: 15 kg/ha.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1: Laser-grade contour bund and swale earthworks. Seed swale immediately after grading; plant bund whips in next planting season (Oct–March). Year 2–3: Spot weed bund plants; suppress competitive vegetation around whip bases. Long-term: Alder/Willow bund maintained as permanent uncut feature. Swale mown annually (August) and biomass removed to prevent P saturation. Inspect bund integrity and repair any rill breaches annually.
registry.rootArchitecture: Biodrilling & Pumping (bund): Alder/Willow roots on the bund penetrate 40–80cm into the constructed earthwork, providing structural stability against slump and piping failure. Alder fixes nitrogen; keep it a minor component where nitrate is a concern. Willow lateral mats bind the outer bund face against spate scour. Swale: Dense rhizomatous and fibrous grass roots (0–15cm) bind the swale base, resisting scouring from ponded flow events.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Ecotone Creation: The wet-to-dry transition between swale (seasonally inundated) and bund (moist but free-draining) creates a species-rich microhabitat mosaic. Wet meadow swale supports aquatic invertebrates, frogs, and dragonflies. Alder/Willow bund provides pollen and winter cover for bumble bees and overwintering beneficial insects.
registry.waterImpacts: Runoff Interception and Detention: Engineered contour bund physically intercepts high-velocity overland flow at the slope mid-point, routing water into the detention swale. Swale holds water for 6–48 hours during storm events, allowing sediment sedimentation and infiltration. Completely disconnects the overland flow hydrological pathway before water exits the productive field. Peak-flow effects are site-specific and unquantified here.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Coastal and estuarine riparian zones in the East Neuk Coast biome subject to saltwater spray and storm surge risk. registry.biodiversityImpacts: Habitat Mosaic: Combines highly disturbed, coppiced habitat (beaver driven) with mature, undisturbed canopy.
registry.waterImpacts: Spate Management: Beaver activity in Zone 1 increases hydrological roughness, slowing flow and recharging groundwater. Note: on small watercourses prone to summer drying (e.g. small burns in the East Neuk Coast biome), mature riparian woodland can increase evapotranspiration demand and may exacerbate low-flow conditions. Where summer low-flow is the primary concern, leaky woody dams, upstream infiltration interventions, and treelines set back from the burn edge are preferred over dense riparian canopy planting on the burn bank itself (SAC agronomist review, April 2026).

registry.soilTypeCondition: Free-draining sandy loams and coastal clay-loams. Land Classes 1–3. Install on the northern or eastern boundary of arable fields most exposed to Haar-driven evaporative stress and salt damage.
registry.plantingRegime: 2 rows plus infill. Mix: 40% Sycamore, 30% Beech, 30% Austrian Pine. Density: 2,500 SPH at 2m × 2m spacing. Plant as 1-year transplants. Nurse planting of faster-establishing Sycamore in outer row to protect slower-establishing Beech and Pine from early wind damage.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1–3: Tree guards (1.2m heavy-duty mesh) essential for all stock. Spot weed around base of trees. Year 4–7: Formative pruning to develop clear, wind-firm single stems; remove co-dominant leaders. Year 8+: High-prune outer Sycamore rows to 2m clear stem to maintain understory airflow and prevent waterlogging. Long-term: No harvest (permanent windbreak function). Selective removal of dead or failing individuals only. No coppice rotation — the windbreak function requires permanent canopy.
registry.rootArchitecture: Sycamore: dense heart-root system 60–90cm depth; provides mid-soil structural stability and moderate hydraulic redistribution. Beech: wide-spreading lateral roots (0–50cm); binds headland soil; leaf litter creates deep forest floor organic layer for SOC accumulation. Austrian/Scots Pine: taproot to 1m+ in freely-draining sandy soils; excellent drought tolerance; root exudates improve mycorrhizal networks in adjacent arable soils.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Specialist Invertebrate Habitat: Beech mast provides critical autumn food resource for Great Tit, Chaffinch, and Brambling. Pine needles and cones support specialist insect communities. Sycamore aphid colonies support a rich food web of natural enemy insects, bats, and small birds. Overall biodiversity is lower than native mixed woodland due to limited species diversity, but the dense structural complexity provides valuable nesting and foraging for common farmland birds.
registry.waterImpacts: Thermal Shelter and Microclimate: Reduces wind speed across a zone 10–20× canopy height, lowering evapotranspiration from adjacent crops. Reduces dew point stress and morning frost incidence on the lee side. Does not provide significant direct water quality benefit (no specialist N-fixing or P-trapping species). Indirect benefit: reduced soil erosion through lower wind-driven surface crust disruption.

registry.agronomicUtility: Protection against spring Haar, salt-spray windburn, and early-season cold north-easterly gusts. GDD uplift in the lee zone: a possible lee-zone warming effect (unquantified for Fife; scenario only). Reduces crop lodging frequency by lowering peak gust speeds at ear height by 30–50% within 10× canopy height. Provides year-round livestock shelter (dairy heat stress reduction in summer via shade; lamb/calf protection in spring via wind reduction).

registry.soilTypeCondition: Wider riparian margins on lower Dreel Burn reaches and coastal burn systems where field geometry permits a 60m riparian zone. Alluvial sandy loams and coastal clay-loams. Priority: productive farmland adjacencies where repeated bank erosion or LWD deficit is reducing watercourse ecological quality.
registry.plantingRegime: Three-zone planting. Zone 1 (0–10m from watercourse): Alder (Alnus glutinosa) 50%, Willow (Salix fragilis/viminalis) 30%, Bird Cherry (Prunus padus) 20%. Density: 2,500 SPH at 2m × 2m spacing. Zone 2 (10–57m from watercourse): Pedunculate Oak (Quercus robur) 30%, Downy Birch (Betula pubescens) 25%, Alder 20%, Willow coppice 15%, Wild Cherry (Prunus avium) 10%. Density: 2,500 SPH. Zone 3 (57–60m, field-side grass buffer): Sown. Mix: 60% Creeping Red Fescue, 30% Cocksfoot, 10% White Clover. Density: 20 kg/ha.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1–3: Tree guards on all Zone 1 and Zone 2 plants. Spot weed around stems. Zone 3: annual mow and remove after 15 August. Year 4+: Remove tree guards once established. Zone 1 left largely unmanaged; natural senescence and LWD recruitment to watercourse is the management objective — do not remove fallen trees from the watercourse. Zone 2: selective timber extraction every 15–20 years under good forestry practice. Clear-fell bays of 0.5ha maximum are acceptable with replanting of felled area. Zone 2 income from Oak and Cherry timber offsets land take costs over 30–50 year period. Zone 3: annual mow and bale to maintain sward density and export P. Do not allow Zone 3 to scrub over — maintain as permanent grass buffer.
registry.rootArchitecture: Zone 1: alder roots fix nitrogen, which can raise nitrate; keep alder to 10-20% where nitrate is the target. Willow develops extensive lateral root mats (0–40cm) with high transpiration capacity. Zone 2 — Structural Anchors: Oak develops deep primary taproot (1.5m+) providing bank anchoring and hydraulic redistribution. Birch lateral roots stabilise mid-bank. Wild Cherry deep taproot contributes to compaction biodrilling. Zone 3 — Surface Binders: Creeping Red Fescue and Cocksfoot dense fibrous root mat (0–15cm) binds the outermost bank and traps overland flow particles.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Maximum Riparian Habitat Quality: Sheridan three-zone design achieves the full suite of riparian ecological functions that smaller buffers cannot. Zone 1 Alder/Willow provides primary salmonid shading (target <16°C summer water temperature), aquatic invertebrate food input via leaf litter, and Dipper/Kingfisher/Otter foraging habitat. Zone 2 mixed woodland creates 3-tier canopy structure supporting woodland specialist species (Wood Warbler, Redstart, Tawny Owl, Brown Long-eared Bat). Zone 3 grass creates the highest-value riparian ecotone gradient: open-to-canopy transition with floral resource for pollinators and seed-eating farmland birds. Large Woody Debris from Zone 2 natural senescence creates critical in-stream habitat for juvenile salmonids and invertebrates (documented in Riverwoods for Scotland 2022, Broadmeadow & Nisbet 2004).
registry.waterImpacts: Maximum Catchment Hydraulic Function: Zone 1 bank-binding prevents lateral erosion. Zone 2 woodland creates high Manning's n roughness across the full 60m width, slowing both overland flow and floodplain inundation events. Large woody debris from Zone 2 increases in-channel retention time, recharging groundwater during moderate events. Zone 3 grass provides the primary particulate phosphorus trap. Note: on very small burns prone to summer drying, the combined transpiration demand of Zone 1+2 may reduce summer baseflows — this variant is most appropriate where the watercourse is of sufficient scale to absorb the evapotranspiration demand of mature riparian woodland without exacerbating low-flow (SAC agronomist review, April 2026). For small East Neuk burns: prefer Variant 19 (20m) or Variant 16 (Planted Contour Swale) over this variant.

Shown for comparison only; excluded from carbon value and net units pending reconstruction.
registry.agronomicUtility: Land Revaluation and Timber Income: Zone 2 provides a long-term timber asset (Oak and Cherry) that offsets income foregone over a 30–50 year period. Zone 3 grass provides annual mowing income as hay/bedding (£30–50/100m/yr). Shelter effects on yield vary: a synthesis of 60 studies found lower yields within about 2 tree heights and small gains further out (Van Vooren et al. 2017). Flood risk reduction: most significant land protection function — prevents progressive loss of productive agricultural land to watercourse lateral migration and bank collapse. Note: the 60m footprint represents a significant permanent land-take. Grant support and timber income are possible but not confirmed. Best suited to farms where: (a) the riparian margin is already low-productivity, (b) the field geometry permits a 60m buffer without severing productive field blocks, or (c) the watercourse carries high flood risk making the riparian margin uninsurable for productive agriculture.

Local provenance, from the NatureScot native list. It meets the AECS rule of at least three native flowering species (AECS guidance gives 60-80% hawthorn as a typical, not required, mix) and is intended to establish at least 4 woody species per 30 m. Spatial planting, survival and survey evidence are needed to confirm species richness.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1: mulch and weed control. Year 2: cut back hard to 45-60 cm to thicken the base. Then trim 1 Dec to end Feb on a 2-3 year rotation, never the same length every year, raising the cut about 10 cm each time; managed at about 2 m wide and 2-2.5 m tall. Margin: low-productivity grass mix with at least four flowering species; no fertiliser or sprays; cut after 15 August with cuttings removed. Do not plant on peat deeper than 30 cm or in fields used by breeding waders.
registry.rootArchitecture: Two rows of fibrous hawthorn and blackthorn roots binding the topsoil, with hazel and holly rooting deeper.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Species-rich native hedgerow (SSE distinctiveness Medium (4)). Screening SSE units: 6.7-7.82 hedgerow units/km at Moderate-Good condition (5-12 years to target). Separate area-unit examples assume an entirely cereal baseline, not this parcel: 1.67 area units/km as arable margin (4.23-5.76 if accepted as neutral grassland).
registry.waterImpacts: 10 m strip: indicative retention of about 83% of sediment and 74% of total phosphorus reaching it (Stutter et al. 2021 width-only fits; soil and slope matter more). Best value where the strip lies across the flow path.
registry.carbonAgronomicAssumptions: Carbon profile: provisional lower-end literature estimate (hedge_carbon_model.py v2 / hedge-config.js). 2 m crown; 50-year gross 52.5 tCO2e/km (biomass 24.5, roots 12, soil 15.9). Grass margin soil carbon is not counted (scenario 22.4-40 tCO2e/km). Not validated; site soil measurement replaces the soil term.
registry.agronomicUtility: Hedge centre 1 m from the boundary; 8 m of grass margin on the field side.
registry.regulatoryAlignment: Possible AECS route (rates checked 3 Nov 2026; pages dated 15 Dec 2025): Planting or Replanting of Hedges (capital GBP5.40/m) with Creation of Hedgerows (GBP1.20/m/yr). Item requirements: double-staggered rows at 6 plants/m and at least three different native flowering species (AECS guidance gives 60-80% hawthorn as a typical mix, not a requirement); livestock fencing at least 1 m from the centre line. Other conditions include in-bye land linked to habitat, no breeding-wader fields, and AECS Creation trimming only from 1 December to the end of February, and not the same length every year; the wider GAEC nesting restriction also applies. Strip: Grass Strips in Arable Fields (target areas only; paid only beyond 2 m from the hedge centre), about 7 m payable, about GBP347/km/yr at GBP495.62/ha/yr. GAEC 7 applies. Eligibility is not confirmed for any site. Using a grant may affect ONCRA eligibility (Guidelines 27 Mar 2026 s4.2.1, s8.2.2): a written ONCRA ruling is needed before grants and carbon units are combined.
registry.additionality: Not assessed. ONCRA financial additionality (Guidelines s8.2.1) and regulatory additionality (s8.2.2), including the government-grant clause (s4.2.1), are unresolved for this activity and need a written ONCRA ruling. Any biodiversity or water benefit claim needs a measured baseline and verification.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Riparian margins, seasonally wet field corners, and ditch-adjacent positions with high nitrate loading from adjacent arable land. NVZ-designated land. Suitable for gleyed soils, wet clay-loams, and permanently moist alluvial soils where standing water is present for at least part of the year. Not suitable for freely-draining soils where wet-soil Alder will fail to establish.
registry.plantingRegime: 2 Rows (staggered). Mix: 50% Alder (Alnus glutinosa), 50% Willow (Salix viminalis or Salix fragilis). Density: 3,000 SPH. Spacing: 1m x 0.6m staggered. Select Fife local provenance Alder where available. Wet-soil tolerant planting stock essential — containerised or bare-root from specialist native nursery.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1: Weed suppression around stems; no cultivation. Year 2–3: Remove dead stock and replace failures. Long-term: No routine harvesting required. Managed as a long-term nitrate interception buffer. Optional management: light coppice of willow every 7–10 years if height management required for adjacent field operations. Keep alder a minor component (10-20%): it fixes nitrogen and can add nitrate (UKFS riparian woodland guide 2024, p.19). Biomass from any willow coppice: chipped for local biomass use.
registry.rootArchitecture: Alder roots host nitrogen-fixing Frankia; fixed nitrogen can raise nitrate leaching (UKFS 2024 p.19), so alder is kept to 10-20% in nitrate-targeted strips. Willow develops extensive lateral root mats (0–40cm) with high transpiration capacity, actively pumping excess soil moisture and dissolved nitrate from the saturated root zone. Combined root system creates a persistent biological barrier intercepting subsurface nitrate leachate pathways.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Wetland Edge Habitat: Alder and Willow provide year-round riparian structure — Willow catkins are the primary early-season pollen source for bumblebees; Alder provides cone seed for siskins and redpolls; wet soil conditions support water vole, frog, newt, and aquatic invertebrate populations. Canopy shading of the adjacent watercourse helps maintain summer water temperature below critical thresholds for aquatic life.
registry.waterImpacts: Maximum Nitrate Interception: Alder root nodule N-fixation prevents net nitrate leaching from the buffer zone itself; Willow lateral roots actively pump dissolved nitrate from subsurface leachate pathways; wet soil denitrification by anaerobic bacteria in the saturated root zone converts residual nitrate to nitrogen gas. Combined mechanisms achieve near-100% nitrate interception efficiency in the riparian position (sepaMetrics nitrateRetention=100). This is the highest-performance NVZ compliance feature in the database.

Can help meet General Binding Rules on diffuse pollution; it does not replace them. Supports WFD Good Ecological Status progression for the Dreel Burn. Adjacent soil N-fixation reduces fertiliser requirement on adjoining fields over time.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Improved pasture and dairy grazing land, particularly south- and west-facing fields exposed to summer afternoon sun. Suitable for Land Classes 2–4 on loamy to clay-loam pasture soils. Priority locations: dairy units with documented summer heat stress indicators (reduced milk yield, somatic cell count increases, reduced conception rates in July–August).
registry.plantingRegime: Open-grown single or double row. Mix: 40% Sycamore (Acer pseudoplatanus), 40% Pedunculate Oak (Quercus robur), 20% Hornbeam (Carpinus betulus). Density: 1 tree per 5–6m. SPH: ~350–400. Wide spacing essential to maximise individual crown development and ground-level light penetration to maintain pasture productivity beneath canopy.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1–5: Vole guards, tree stakes, and spot weed suppression around base. Year 3–7: Formative pruning to develop high crown (clear stem to 2–2.5m) ensuring unimpeded airflow and livestock access to shade without bark damage. Long-term: Annual inspection for storm damage; remove epicormic growth from lower stem. Biomass: Timber asset managed under long-term schedule; no routine harvest. Root-blading optional at Year 10+ if pasture productivity under canopy requires renovation.
registry.rootArchitecture: Deep Taproots: Oak develops a primary taproot to 1.5m+ depth in well-structured soils, bypassing the shallow grass root zone and drawing deep groundwater via hydraulic redistribution during summer drought. Sycamore develops a heart-root system to 80–100cm. Hornbeam lateral roots provide mid-depth pasture stabilisation. Combined deep root architecture maximises hydraulic lift to maintain adjacent pasture soil moisture during the critical July–August drought period in the East Neuk.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Thermogenesis Corridor: Mature oak canopy supports 280+ associated invertebrate species — the highest of any native tree. Hollow trunks and dead wood in mature trees provide bat roost opportunities. Open-grown sycamore provides significant aphid resource for insectivorous birds. Connects isolated pasture habitats for barn owls, bats, and avian predators hunting rodents in the field margin.
registry.waterImpacts: Drought Buffering: Deep taproot hydraulic redistribution maintains pasture soil moisture during summer drought, reducing crop and pasture stress (see droughtResilience score=80). Canopy cooling (3.75°C below ambient on hot days; Burschel & Huss 1997) reduces evapotranspiration from the shaded zone and reduces livestock heat stress. Shade also reduces soil moisture loss through surface evaporation in the shade zone.

Reduces somatic cell counts associated with heat stress mastitis risk. Long-term timber asset from Oak.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Long, unbroken sloping arable fields (Land Classes 2–4) with overland surface runoff and rill erosion risk. Contour swales are most effective on slopes of 2–8° where laser-graded earthworks can direct and detain flow. Priority: fields with documented gully formation, compacted headlands, or watercourse siltation downstream.
registry.plantingRegime: Zoned earthworks planting. Bund (upper edge, 2m width): 100% SRC Alder (Alnus glutinosa) and Willow (Salix viminalis mix) at 10,000 SPH for immediate root stabilisation of the constructed bund. Swale (6m detention zone): sown wet-meadow grass mix — Meadowsweet, Flote-grass, Yorkshire Fog, Red Fescue — to maximise roughness and FIO trapping. Bund plants: 1-year whip, bare-root. Swale seed: 15 kg/ha.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1: Laser-grade contour bund and swale earthworks. Seed swale immediately after grading; plant bund whips in next planting season (Oct–March). Year 2–3: Spot weed bund plants; suppress competitive vegetation around whip bases. Long-term: Alder/Willow bund maintained as permanent uncut feature. Swale mown annually (August) and biomass removed to prevent P saturation. Inspect bund integrity and repair any rill breaches annually.
registry.rootArchitecture: Biodrilling & Pumping (bund): Alder/Willow roots on the bund penetrate 40–80cm into the constructed earthwork, providing structural stability against slump and piping failure. Alder fixes nitrogen; keep it a minor component where nitrate is a concern. Willow lateral mats bind the outer bund face against spate scour. Swale: Dense rhizomatous and fibrous grass roots (0–15cm) bind the swale base, resisting scouring from ponded flow events.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Ecotone Creation: The wet-to-dry transition between swale (seasonally inundated) and bund (moist but free-draining) creates a species-rich microhabitat mosaic. Wet meadow swale supports aquatic invertebrates, frogs, and dragonflies. Alder/Willow bund provides pollen and winter cover for bumble bees and overwintering beneficial insects.
registry.waterImpacts: Runoff Interception and Detention: Engineered contour bund physically intercepts high-velocity overland flow at the slope mid-point, routing water into the detention swale. Swale holds water for 6–48 hours during storm events, allowing sediment sedimentation and infiltration. Completely disconnects the overland flow hydrological pathway before water exits the productive field. Peak-flow effects are site-specific and unquantified here.

Harvest: stems felled autumn, field-dried through summer, chipped following autumn. Species: Birch 60% (fast growth; excellent pyrolysis char yield); Alder 30% (N-fixation; good char); Wild Cherry 10% (structure and biodiversity). Biochar application to adjacent arable at 5-10 t/ha per 10-year cycle. Farm-scale Kon-Tiki or ring kiln most practical for strip-scale volumes.

registry.waterImpacts: Extreme Bio-Pumping: Rapid transpiration system designed to "drink" wet clays, while the harvested biochar acts as an ultimate flood-delay sponge when applied to soil.

registry.rootArchitecture: Sycamore: dense heart-root system 60–90cm depth; provides mid-soil structural stability and moderate hydraulic redistribution. Beech: wide-spreading lateral roots (0–50cm); binds headland soil; leaf litter creates deep forest floor organic layer for SOC accumulation. Austrian/Scots Pine: taproot to 1m+ in freely-draining sandy soils; excellent drought tolerance; root exudates improve mycorrhizal networks in adjacent arable soils.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Specialist Invertebrate Habitat: Beech mast provides critical autumn food resource for Great Tit, Chaffinch, and Brambling. Pine needles and cones support specialist insect communities. Sycamore aphid colonies support a rich food web of natural enemy insects, bats, and small birds. Overall biodiversity is lower than native mixed woodland due to limited species diversity, but the dense structural complexity provides valuable nesting and foraging for common farmland birds.
registry.waterImpacts: Thermal Shelter and Microclimate: Reduces wind speed across a zone 10–20× canopy height, lowering evapotranspiration from adjacent crops. Indirect benefit: reduced soil erosion through lower wind-driven surface crust disruption.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Urban fringe riparian margins where planning permissions and available land permit significant riparian woodland creation. Variable soils. Priority: watercourses with urban flood risk and high public amenity value where LWD and canopy cover can improve ecological status and resilience.
registry.plantingRegime: Three-zone planting. Zone 1 (0–10m from watercourse): Alder (Alnus glutinosa) 50%, Willow (Salix fragilis/viminalis) 30%, Bird Cherry (Prunus padus) 20%. Density: 2,500 SPH at 2m × 2m spacing. Zone 2 (10–57m from watercourse): Pedunculate Oak (Quercus robur) 30%, Downy Birch (Betula pubescens) 25%, Alder 20%, Willow coppice 15%, Wild Cherry (Prunus avium) 10%. Density: 2,500 SPH. Zone 3 (57–60m, field-side grass buffer): Sown. Mix: 60% Creeping Red Fescue, 30% Cocksfoot, 10% White Clover. Density: 20 kg/ha.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1–3: Tree guards on all Zone 1 and Zone 2 plants. Spot weed around stems. Zone 3: annual mow and remove after 15 August. Year 4+: Remove tree guards once established. Zone 1 left largely unmanaged; natural senescence and LWD recruitment to watercourse is the management objective — do not remove fallen trees from the watercourse. Zone 2: selective timber extraction every 15–20 years under good forestry practice. Clear-fell bays of 0.5ha maximum are acceptable with replanting of felled area. Zone 2 income from Oak and Cherry timber offsets land take costs over 30–50 year period. Zone 3: annual mow and bale to maintain sward density and export P. Do not allow Zone 3 to scrub over — maintain as permanent grass buffer.
registry.rootArchitecture: Zone 1: alder roots fix nitrogen, which can raise nitrate; keep alder to 10-20% where nitrate is the target. Willow develops extensive lateral root mats (0–40cm) with high transpiration capacity. Zone 2 — Structural Anchors: Oak develops deep primary taproot (1.5m+) providing bank anchoring and hydraulic redistribution. Birch lateral roots stabilise mid-bank. Wild Cherry deep taproot contributes to compaction biodrilling. Zone 3 — Surface Binders: Creeping Red Fescue and Cocksfoot dense fibrous root mat (0–15cm) binds the outermost bank and traps overland flow particles.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Maximum Riparian Habitat Quality: Sheridan three-zone design achieves the full suite of riparian ecological functions that smaller buffers cannot. Zone 1 Alder/Willow provides primary salmonid shading (target <16°C summer water temperature), aquatic invertebrate food input via leaf litter, and Dipper/Kingfisher/Otter foraging habitat. Zone 2 mixed woodland creates 3-tier canopy structure supporting woodland specialist species (Wood Warbler, Redstart, Tawny Owl, Brown Long-eared Bat). Zone 3 grass creates the highest-value riparian ecotone gradient: open-to-canopy transition with floral resource for pollinators and seed-eating farmland birds. Large Woody Debris from Zone 2 natural senescence creates critical in-stream habitat for juvenile salmonids and invertebrates (documented in Riverwoods for Scotland 2022, Broadmeadow & Nisbet 2004).
registry.waterImpacts: Maximum Catchment Hydraulic Function: Zone 1 bank-binding prevents lateral erosion. Zone 2 woodland creates high Manning's n roughness across the full 60m width, slowing both overland flow and floodplain inundation events. Large woody debris from Zone 2 increases in-channel retention time, recharging groundwater during moderate events. Zone 3 grass provides the primary particulate phosphorus trap. Note: on very small burns prone to summer drying, the combined transpiration demand of Zone 1+2 may reduce summer baseflows — this variant is most appropriate where the watercourse is of sufficient scale to absorb the evapotranspiration demand of mature riparian woodland without exacerbating low-flow (SAC agronomist review, April 2026). For small East Neuk burns: prefer Variant 19 (20m) or Variant 16 (Planted Contour Swale) over this variant.

registry.agronomicUtility: Land Revaluation and Timber Income: Zone 2 provides a long-term timber asset (Oak and Cherry) that offsets income foregone over a 30–50 year period. Zone 3 grass provides annual mowing income as hay/bedding (£30–50/100m/yr). Shelter effects on yield vary: a synthesis of 60 studies found lower yields within about 2 tree heights and small gains further out (Van Vooren et al. 2017). Flood risk reduction: most significant land protection function — prevents progressive loss of productive agricultural land to watercourse lateral migration and bank collapse. Note: the 60m footprint represents a significant permanent land-take. Grant support and timber income are possible but not confirmed. Best suited to farms where: (a) the riparian margin is already low-productivity, (b) the field geometry permits a 60m buffer without severing productive field blocks, or (c) the watercourse carries high flood risk making the riparian margin uninsurable for productive agriculture.

Local provenance, from the NatureScot native list. It meets the AECS rule of at least three native flowering species (AECS guidance gives 60-80% hawthorn as a typical, not required, mix) and is intended to establish at least 4 woody species per 30 m. Spatial planting, survival and survey evidence are needed to confirm species richness.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1: mulch and weed control. Year 2: cut back hard to 45-60 cm to thicken the base. Then trim 1 Dec to end Feb on a 2-3 year rotation, never the same length every year, raising the cut about 10 cm each time; managed at about 2 m wide and 2-2.5 m tall. Margin: low-productivity grass mix with at least four flowering species; no fertiliser or sprays; cut after 15 August with cuttings removed. Do not plant on peat deeper than 30 cm or in fields used by breeding waders.
registry.rootArchitecture: Two rows of fibrous hawthorn and blackthorn roots binding the topsoil, with hazel and holly rooting deeper.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Species-rich native hedgerow (SSE distinctiveness Medium (4)). Screening SSE units: 6.7-7.82 hedgerow units/km at Moderate-Good condition (5-12 years to target). Separate area-unit examples assume an entirely cereal baseline, not this parcel: 1.67 area units/km as arable margin (4.23-5.76 if accepted as neutral grassland).
registry.waterImpacts: 10 m strip: indicative retention of about 83% of sediment and 74% of total phosphorus reaching it (Stutter et al. 2021 width-only fits; soil and slope matter more). Best value where the strip lies across the flow path.
registry.carbonAgronomicAssumptions: Carbon profile: provisional lower-end literature estimate (hedge_carbon_model.py v2 / hedge-config.js). 2 m crown; 50-year gross 52.5 tCO2e/km (biomass 24.5, roots 12, soil 15.9). Grass margin soil carbon is not counted (scenario 22.4-40 tCO2e/km). Not validated; site soil measurement replaces the soil term.
registry.agronomicUtility: Hedge centre 1 m from the boundary; 8 m of grass margin on the field side.
registry.regulatoryAlignment: Possible AECS route (rates checked 3 Nov 2026; pages dated 15 Dec 2025): Planting or Replanting of Hedges (capital GBP5.40/m) with Creation of Hedgerows (GBP1.20/m/yr). Item requirements: double-staggered rows at 6 plants/m and at least three different native flowering species (AECS guidance gives 60-80% hawthorn as a typical mix, not a requirement); livestock fencing at least 1 m from the centre line. Other conditions include in-bye land linked to habitat, no breeding-wader fields, and AECS Creation trimming only from 1 December to the end of February, and not the same length every year; the wider GAEC nesting restriction also applies. Strip: Grass Strips in Arable Fields (target areas only; paid only beyond 2 m from the hedge centre), about 7 m payable, about GBP347/km/yr at GBP495.62/ha/yr. GAEC 7 applies. Eligibility is not confirmed for any site. Using a grant may affect ONCRA eligibility (Guidelines 27 Mar 2026 s4.2.1, s8.2.2): a written ONCRA ruling is needed before grants and carbon units are combined.
registry.additionality: Not assessed. ONCRA financial additionality (Guidelines s8.2.1) and regulatory additionality (s8.2.2), including the government-grant clause (s4.2.1), are unresolved for this activity and need a written ONCRA ruling. Any biodiversity or water benefit claim needs a measured baseline and verification.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Riparian margins, seasonally wet field corners, and ditch-adjacent positions with high nitrate loading from adjacent arable land. NVZ-designated land. Suitable for gleyed soils, wet clay-loams, and permanently moist alluvial soils where standing water is present for at least part of the year. Not suitable for freely-draining soils where wet-soil Alder will fail to establish.
registry.plantingRegime: 2 Rows (staggered). Mix: 50% Alder (Alnus glutinosa), 50% Willow (Salix viminalis or Salix fragilis). Density: 3,000 SPH. Spacing: 1m x 0.6m staggered. Select Fife local provenance Alder where available. Wet-soil tolerant planting stock essential — containerised or bare-root from specialist native nursery.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1: Weed suppression around stems; no cultivation. Year 2–3: Remove dead stock and replace failures. Long-term: No routine harvesting required. Managed as a long-term nitrate interception buffer. Optional management: light coppice of willow every 7–10 years if height management required for adjacent field operations. Keep alder a minor component (10-20%): it fixes nitrogen and can add nitrate (UKFS riparian woodland guide 2024, p.19). Biomass from any willow coppice: chipped for local biomass use.
registry.rootArchitecture: Alder roots host nitrogen-fixing Frankia; fixed nitrogen can raise nitrate leaching (UKFS 2024 p.19), so alder is kept to 10-20% in nitrate-targeted strips. Willow develops extensive lateral root mats (0–40cm) with high transpiration capacity, actively pumping excess soil moisture and dissolved nitrate from the saturated root zone. Combined root system creates a persistent biological barrier intercepting subsurface nitrate leachate pathways.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Wetland Edge Habitat: Alder and Willow provide year-round riparian structure — Willow catkins are the primary early-season pollen source for bumblebees; Alder provides cone seed for siskins and redpolls; wet soil conditions support water vole, frog, newt, and aquatic invertebrate populations. Canopy shading of the adjacent watercourse helps maintain summer water temperature below critical thresholds for aquatic life.
registry.waterImpacts: Maximum Nitrate Interception: Alder root nodule N-fixation prevents net nitrate leaching from the buffer zone itself; Willow lateral roots actively pump dissolved nitrate from subsurface leachate pathways; wet soil denitrification by anaerobic bacteria in the saturated root zone converts residual nitrate to nitrogen gas. Combined mechanisms achieve near-100% nitrate interception efficiency in the riparian position (sepaMetrics nitrateRetention=100). This is the highest-performance NVZ compliance feature in the database.

Can help meet General Binding Rules on diffuse pollution; it does not replace them. Supports WFD Good Ecological Status progression for the Dreel Burn. Adjacent soil N-fixation reduces fertiliser requirement on adjoining fields over time.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Improved pasture and dairy grazing land, particularly south- and west-facing fields exposed to summer afternoon sun. Suitable for Land Classes 2–4 on loamy to clay-loam pasture soils. Priority locations: dairy units with documented summer heat stress indicators (reduced milk yield, somatic cell count increases, reduced conception rates in July–August).
registry.plantingRegime: Open-grown single or double row. Mix: 40% Sycamore (Acer pseudoplatanus), 40% Pedunculate Oak (Quercus robur), 20% Hornbeam (Carpinus betulus). Density: 1 tree per 5–6m. SPH: ~350–400. Wide spacing essential to maximise individual crown development and ground-level light penetration to maintain pasture productivity beneath canopy.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1–5: Vole guards, tree stakes, and spot weed suppression around base. Year 3–7: Formative pruning to develop high crown (clear stem to 2–2.5m) ensuring unimpeded airflow and livestock access to shade without bark damage. Long-term: Annual inspection for storm damage; remove epicormic growth from lower stem. Biomass: Timber asset managed under long-term schedule; no routine harvest. Root-blading optional at Year 10+ if pasture productivity under canopy requires renovation.
registry.rootArchitecture: Deep Taproots: Oak develops a primary taproot to 1.5m+ depth in well-structured soils, bypassing the shallow grass root zone and drawing deep groundwater via hydraulic redistribution during summer drought. Sycamore develops a heart-root system to 80–100cm. Hornbeam lateral roots provide mid-depth pasture stabilisation. Combined deep root architecture maximises hydraulic lift to maintain adjacent pasture soil moisture during the critical July–August drought period in the East Neuk.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Thermogenesis Corridor: Mature oak canopy supports 280+ associated invertebrate species — the highest of any native tree. Hollow trunks and dead wood in mature trees provide bat roost opportunities. Open-grown sycamore provides significant aphid resource for insectivorous birds. Connects isolated pasture habitats for barn owls, bats, and avian predators hunting rodents in the field margin.
registry.waterImpacts: Drought Buffering: Deep taproot hydraulic redistribution maintains pasture soil moisture during summer drought, reducing crop and pasture stress (see droughtResilience score=80). Canopy cooling (3.75°C below ambient on hot days; Burschel & Huss 1997) reduces evapotranspiration from the shaded zone and reduces livestock heat stress. Shade also reduces soil moisture loss through surface evaporation in the shade zone.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Long, unbroken sloping arable fields (Land Classes 2–4) with overland surface runoff and rill erosion risk. Contour swales are most effective on slopes of 2–8° where laser-graded earthworks can direct and detain flow. Priority: fields with documented gully formation, compacted headlands, or watercourse siltation downstream.
registry.plantingRegime: Zoned earthworks planting. Bund (upper edge, 2m width): 100% SRC Alder (Alnus glutinosa) and Willow (Salix viminalis mix) at 10,000 SPH for immediate root stabilisation of the constructed bund. Swale (6m detention zone): sown wet-meadow grass mix — Meadowsweet, Flote-grass, Yorkshire Fog, Red Fescue — to maximise roughness and FIO trapping. Bund plants: 1-year whip, bare-root. Swale seed: 15 kg/ha.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1: Laser-grade contour bund and swale earthworks. Seed swale immediately after grading; plant bund whips in next planting season (Oct–March). Year 2–3: Spot weed bund plants; suppress competitive vegetation around whip bases. Long-term: Alder/Willow bund maintained as permanent uncut feature. Swale mown annually (August) and biomass removed to prevent P saturation. Inspect bund integrity and repair any rill breaches annually.
registry.rootArchitecture: Biodrilling & Pumping (bund): Alder/Willow roots on the bund penetrate 40–80cm into the constructed earthwork, providing structural stability against slump and piping failure. Alder fixes nitrogen; keep it a minor component where nitrate is a concern. Willow lateral mats bind the outer bund face against spate scour. Swale: Dense rhizomatous and fibrous grass roots (0–15cm) bind the swale base, resisting scouring from ponded flow events.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Ecotone Creation: The wet-to-dry transition between swale (seasonally inundated) and bund (moist but free-draining) creates a species-rich microhabitat mosaic. Wet meadow swale supports aquatic invertebrates, frogs, and dragonflies. Alder/Willow bund provides pollen and winter cover for bumble bees and overwintering beneficial insects.
registry.waterImpacts: Runoff Interception and Detention: Engineered contour bund physically intercepts high-velocity overland flow at the slope mid-point, routing water into the detention swale. Swale holds water for 6–48 hours during storm events, allowing sediment sedimentation and infiltration. Completely disconnects the overland flow hydrological pathway before water exits the productive field. Peak-flow effects are site-specific and unquantified here.

Critical: minimum 6-year rotation is required to permit air-drying of harvested timber to <20% MC in Scottish lowland conditions. Harvest: stems felled autumn, field-dried through summer, chipped following autumn. Species: Birch 60% (fast growth; excellent pyrolysis char yield); Alder 30% (N-fixation; good char); Wild Cherry 10% (structure and biodiversity). Biochar application to adjacent arable at 5-10 t/ha per 10-year cycle. Farm-scale Kon-Tiki or ring kiln most practical for strip-scale volumes.

registry.waterImpacts: Extreme Bio-Pumping: Rapid transpiration system designed to "drink" wet clays, while the harvested biochar acts as an ultimate flood-delay sponge when applied to soil.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Riparian floodplain margins and burn-side zones in the Howe of Fife and Eden catchment where bank stabilisation and flow roughness are the primary objectives. Wet alluvial soils, seasonally inundated floodplain. Priority: unstable banks on productive farmland adjacencies where watercourse erosion threatens field boundaries. Note: suitable for reaches where beavers are present or likely; the zoned planting design accommodates browsing without sacrificing the permanent woodland asset.
registry.plantingRegime: Zoned planting. Zone 1 (bank edge, 5m): High-density Willow (Salix viminalis / Salix fragilis mix) at 10,000 SPH — rapid bank-binding and replaceable browse layer. Zone 2 (behind Zone 1, 15m): Sessile Oak and Alder at 2,500 SPH — permanent long-term timber and carbon asset with deep root bank anchoring. SPH: ~1,600 overall per 20m width.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1–3: Heavy-duty tree guards on Zone 2 Oak/Alder. Zone 1 Willow left unguarded as self-establishing bank stabilisation. Long-term: Zone 1 managed as permanent uncut bank-binding feature; Zone 2 managed with minimal intervention except safety pruning. Biomass: natural senescence; trunks left to fall into river as large woody debris. Note on beaver management: if Castor fiber activity is present or anticipated, Zone 1 Willow acts as a sacrificial browse layer, protecting Zone 2 timber asset. Do not present this variant to farmers using the word 'beaver' — discuss as 'bank stabilisation with browse-tolerant outer planting'.
registry.rootArchitecture: Structural Nets: Willow (Zone 1) creates rapid, dense fibrous bank-binding within the first 2 seasons, preventing undercutting and slump. Oak (Zone 2) develops deep structural taproots providing permanent bank anchorage against extreme spate flows. Alder lateral roots fix nitrogen and stabilise mid-bank alluvial sediment layers.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Riparian Habitat Mosaic: Zone 1 dense Willow provides year-round nesting, pollen (catkins), and insect habitat. Zone 2 mature Oak supports 280+ associated invertebrate species. Combined open-to-closed riparian canopy gradient supports full range of Fife riparian priority species including Dipper, Kingfisher, Otter, and Water Vole. Canopy shading of the burn maintains critical summer water temperatures for aquatic invertebrates.
registry.waterImpacts: Bank Stabilisation and Flow Roughness: Willow bank-binding prevents physical erosion of alluvial material into the watercourse. Mature woodland creates high hydraulic roughness, slowing peak flows and increasing detention time. Large woody debris from Zone 2 senescence creates in-channel habitat and further increases roughness. Note: on very small, drought-prone burns, high transpiration demand from mature riparian woodland may reduce summer low-flows — see droughtResilience score and consult SEPA before installation on small-catchment burns with documented summer drying.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Deep productive loams of the Howe of Fife valley floor and lower slopes. Land Classes 1–3. Priority: low-lying fields with documented frost-pocket topography where late spring frost is a recurring crop loss risk.
registry.plantingRegime: 2 rows plus infill. Mix: 40% Sycamore, 40% Beech, 20% Austrian Pine. Density: 2,500 SPH at 2m × 2m spacing. Plant as 1-year transplants. Nurse planting of faster-establishing Sycamore in outer row to protect slower-establishing Beech and Pine from early wind damage.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1–3: Tree guards (1.2m heavy-duty mesh) essential for all stock. Spot weed around base of trees. Year 4–7: Formative pruning to develop clear, wind-firm single stems; remove co-dominant leaders. Year 8+: High-prune outer Sycamore rows to 2m clear stem to maintain understory airflow and prevent waterlogging. Long-term: No harvest (permanent windbreak function). Selective removal of dead or failing individuals only. No coppice rotation — the windbreak function requires permanent canopy.
registry.rootArchitecture: Sycamore: dense heart-root system 60–90cm depth; provides mid-soil structural stability and moderate hydraulic redistribution. Beech: wide-spreading lateral roots (0–50cm); binds headland soil; leaf litter creates deep forest floor organic layer for SOC accumulation. Austrian/Scots Pine: taproot to 1m+ in freely-draining sandy soils; excellent drought tolerance; root exudates improve mycorrhizal networks in adjacent arable soils.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Specialist Invertebrate Habitat: Beech mast provides critical autumn food resource for Great Tit, Chaffinch, and Brambling. Pine needles and cones support specialist insect communities. Sycamore aphid colonies support a rich food web of natural enemy insects, bats, and small birds. Overall biodiversity is lower than native mixed woodland due to limited species diversity, but the dense structural complexity provides valuable nesting and foraging for common farmland birds.
registry.waterImpacts: Thermal Shelter and Microclimate: Reduces wind speed across a zone 10–20× canopy height, lowering evapotranspiration from adjacent crops. Reduces dew point stress and morning frost incidence on the lee side. Does not provide significant direct water quality benefit (no specialist N-fixing or P-trapping species). Indirect benefit: reduced soil erosion through lower wind-driven surface crust disruption.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Eden Water and major Howe of Fife watercourse floodplains where productive farmland borders accessible riparian margins. Deep alluvial loams. The prime Fife candidate biome for this variant: Eden catchment watercourses carry high sediment loads and benefit greatly from wider riparian woodland zones.
registry.plantingRegime: Three-zone planting. Zone 1 (0–10m from watercourse): Alder (Alnus glutinosa) 50%, Willow (Salix fragilis/viminalis) 30%, Bird Cherry (Prunus padus) 20%. Density: 2,500 SPH at 2m × 2m spacing. Zone 2 (10–57m from watercourse): Pedunculate Oak (Quercus robur) 30%, Downy Birch (Betula pubescens) 25%, Alder 20%, Willow coppice 15%, Wild Cherry (Prunus avium) 10%. Density: 2,500 SPH. Zone 3 (57–60m, field-side grass buffer): Sown. Mix: 60% Creeping Red Fescue, 30% Cocksfoot, 10% White Clover. Density: 20 kg/ha.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1–3: Tree guards on all Zone 1 and Zone 2 plants. Spot weed around stems. Zone 3: annual mow and remove after 15 August. Year 4+: Remove tree guards once established. Zone 1 left largely unmanaged; natural senescence and LWD recruitment to watercourse is the management objective — do not remove fallen trees from the watercourse. Zone 2: selective timber extraction every 15–20 years under good forestry practice. Clear-fell bays of 0.5ha maximum are acceptable with replanting of felled area. Zone 2 income from Oak and Cherry timber offsets land take costs over 30–50 year period. Zone 3: annual mow and bale to maintain sward density and export P. Do not allow Zone 3 to scrub over — maintain as permanent grass buffer.
registry.rootArchitecture: Zone 1: alder roots fix nitrogen, which can raise nitrate; keep alder to 10-20% where nitrate is the target. Willow develops extensive lateral root mats (0–40cm) with high transpiration capacity. Zone 2 — Structural Anchors: Oak develops deep primary taproot (1.5m+) providing bank anchoring and hydraulic redistribution. Birch lateral roots stabilise mid-bank. Wild Cherry deep taproot contributes to compaction biodrilling. Zone 3 — Surface Binders: Creeping Red Fescue and Cocksfoot dense fibrous root mat (0–15cm) binds the outermost bank and traps overland flow particles.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Maximum Riparian Habitat Quality: Sheridan three-zone design achieves the full suite of riparian ecological functions that smaller buffers cannot. Zone 1 Alder/Willow provides primary salmonid shading (target <16°C summer water temperature), aquatic invertebrate food input via leaf litter, and Dipper/Kingfisher/Otter foraging habitat. Zone 2 mixed woodland creates 3-tier canopy structure supporting woodland specialist species (Wood Warbler, Redstart, Tawny Owl, Brown Long-eared Bat). Zone 3 grass creates the highest-value riparian ecotone gradient: open-to-canopy transition with floral resource for pollinators and seed-eating farmland birds. Large Woody Debris from Zone 2 natural senescence creates critical in-stream habitat for juvenile salmonids and invertebrates (documented in Riverwoods for Scotland 2022, Broadmeadow & Nisbet 2004).
registry.waterImpacts: Maximum Catchment Hydraulic Function: Zone 1 bank-binding prevents lateral erosion. Zone 2 woodland creates high Manning's n roughness across the full 60m width, slowing both overland flow and floodplain inundation events. Large woody debris from Zone 2 increases in-channel retention time, recharging groundwater during moderate events. Zone 3 grass provides the primary particulate phosphorus trap. Note: on very small burns prone to summer drying, the combined transpiration demand of Zone 1+2 may reduce summer baseflows — this variant is most appropriate where the watercourse is of sufficient scale to absorb the evapotranspiration demand of mature riparian woodland without exacerbating low-flow (SAC agronomist review, April 2026). For small East Neuk burns: prefer Variant 19 (20m) or Variant 16 (Planted Contour Swale) over this variant.

registry.agronomicUtility: Land Revaluation and Timber Income: Zone 2 provides a long-term timber asset (Oak and Cherry) that offsets income foregone over a 30–50 year period. Zone 3 grass provides annual mowing income as hay/bedding (£30–50/100m/yr). Shelter effects on yield vary: a synthesis of 60 studies found lower yields within about 2 tree heights and small gains further out (Van Vooren et al. 2017). Flood risk reduction: most significant land protection function — prevents progressive loss of productive agricultural land to watercourse lateral migration and bank collapse. Note: the 60m footprint represents a significant permanent land-take. Grant support and timber income are possible but not confirmed. Best suited to farms where: (a) the riparian margin is already low-productivity, (b) the field geometry permits a 60m buffer without severing productive field blocks, or (c) the watercourse carries high flood risk making the riparian margin uninsurable for productive agriculture.

registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1: Weed suppression around stems; no cultivation. Year 2–3: Remove dead stock and replace failures. Long-term: No routine harvesting required. Managed as a long-term nitrate interception buffer. Optional management: light coppice of willow every 7–10 years if height management required for adjacent field operations. Keep alder a minor component (10-20%): it fixes nitrogen and can add nitrate (UKFS riparian woodland guide 2024, p.19). Biomass from any willow coppice: chipped for local biomass use.
registry.rootArchitecture: Alder roots host nitrogen-fixing Frankia; fixed nitrogen can raise nitrate leaching (UKFS 2024 p.19), so alder is kept to 10-20% in nitrate-targeted strips. Willow develops extensive lateral root mats (0–40cm) with high transpiration capacity, actively pumping excess soil moisture and dissolved nitrate from the saturated root zone. Combined root system creates a persistent biological barrier intercepting subsurface nitrate leachate pathways.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Wetland Edge Habitat: Alder and Willow provide year-round riparian structure — Willow catkins are the primary early-season pollen source for bumblebees; Alder provides cone seed for siskins and redpolls; wet soil conditions support water vole, frog, newt, and aquatic invertebrate populations. Canopy shading of the adjacent watercourse helps maintain summer water temperature below critical thresholds for aquatic life.
registry.waterImpacts: Maximum Nitrate Interception: Alder root nodule N-fixation prevents net nitrate leaching from the buffer zone itself; Willow lateral roots actively pump dissolved nitrate from subsurface leachate pathways; wet soil denitrification by anaerobic bacteria in the saturated root zone converts residual nitrate to nitrogen gas. Combined mechanisms achieve near-100% nitrate interception efficiency in the riparian position (sepaMetrics nitrateRetention=100). This is the highest-performance NVZ compliance feature in the database.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Improved pasture and dairy grazing land, particularly south- and west-facing fields exposed to summer afternoon sun. Suitable for Land Classes 2–4 on loamy to clay-loam pasture soils. Priority locations: dairy units with documented summer heat stress indicators (reduced milk yield, somatic cell count increases, reduced conception rates in July–August).
registry.plantingRegime: Open-grown single or double row. Mix: 40% Sycamore (Acer pseudoplatanus), 40% Pedunculate Oak (Quercus robur), 20% Hornbeam (Carpinus betulus). Density: 1 tree per 5–6m. SPH: ~350–400. Wide spacing essential to maximise individual crown development and ground-level light penetration to maintain pasture productivity beneath canopy.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1–5: Vole guards, tree stakes, and spot weed suppression around base. Year 3–7: Formative pruning to develop high crown (clear stem to 2–2.5m) ensuring unimpeded airflow and livestock access to shade without bark damage. Long-term: Annual inspection for storm damage; remove epicormic growth from lower stem. Biomass: Timber asset managed under long-term schedule; no routine harvest. Root-blading optional at Year 10+ if pasture productivity under canopy requires renovation.
registry.rootArchitecture: Deep Taproots: Oak develops a primary taproot to 1.5m+ depth in well-structured soils, bypassing the shallow grass root zone and drawing deep groundwater via hydraulic redistribution during summer drought. Sycamore develops a heart-root system to 80–100cm. Hornbeam lateral roots provide mid-depth pasture stabilisation. Combined deep root architecture maximises hydraulic lift to maintain adjacent pasture soil moisture during the critical July–August drought period in the East Neuk.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Thermogenesis Corridor: Mature oak canopy supports 280+ associated invertebrate species — the highest of any native tree. Hollow trunks and dead wood in mature trees provide bat roost opportunities. Open-grown sycamore provides significant aphid resource for insectivorous birds. Connects isolated pasture habitats for barn owls, bats, and avian predators hunting rodents in the field margin.
registry.waterImpacts: Drought Buffering: Deep taproot hydraulic redistribution maintains pasture soil moisture during summer drought, reducing crop and pasture stress (see droughtResilience score=80). Canopy cooling (3.75°C below ambient on hot days; Burschel & Huss 1997) reduces evapotranspiration from the shaded zone and reduces livestock heat stress. Shade also reduces soil moisture loss through surface evaporation in the shade zone.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Long, unbroken sloping arable fields (Land Classes 2–4) with overland surface runoff and rill erosion risk. Contour swales are most effective on slopes of 2–8° where laser-graded earthworks can direct and detain flow. Priority: fields with documented gully formation, compacted headlands, or watercourse siltation downstream.
registry.plantingRegime: Zoned earthworks planting. Bund (upper edge, 2m width): 100% SRC Alder (Alnus glutinosa) and Willow (Salix viminalis mix) at 10,000 SPH for immediate root stabilisation of the constructed bund. Swale (6m detention zone): sown wet-meadow grass mix — Meadowsweet, Flote-grass, Yorkshire Fog, Red Fescue — to maximise roughness and FIO trapping. Bund plants: 1-year whip, bare-root. Swale seed: 15 kg/ha.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1: Laser-grade contour bund and swale earthworks. Seed swale immediately after grading; plant bund whips in next planting season (Oct–March). Year 2–3: Spot weed bund plants; suppress competitive vegetation around whip bases. Long-term: Alder/Willow bund maintained as permanent uncut feature. Swale mown annually (August) and biomass removed to prevent P saturation. Inspect bund integrity and repair any rill breaches annually.
registry.rootArchitecture: Biodrilling & Pumping (bund): Alder/Willow roots on the bund penetrate 40–80cm into the constructed earthwork, providing structural stability against slump and piping failure. Alder fixes nitrogen; keep it a minor component where nitrate is a concern. Willow lateral mats bind the outer bund face against spate scour. Swale: Dense rhizomatous and fibrous grass roots (0–15cm) bind the swale base, resisting scouring from ponded flow events.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Ecotone Creation: The wet-to-dry transition between swale (seasonally inundated) and bund (moist but free-draining) creates a species-rich microhabitat mosaic. Wet meadow swale supports aquatic invertebrates, frogs, and dragonflies. Alder/Willow bund provides pollen and winter cover for bumble bees and overwintering beneficial insects.
registry.waterImpacts: Runoff Interception and Detention: Engineered contour bund physically intercepts high-velocity overland flow at the slope mid-point, routing water into the detention swale. Swale holds water for 6–48 hours during storm events, allowing sediment sedimentation and infiltration. Completely disconnects the overland flow hydrological pathway before water exits the productive field. Peak-flow effects are site-specific and unquantified here.

Species: Birch 60% (fast growth; excellent pyrolysis char yield); Alder 30% (N-fixation; good char); Wild Cherry 10% (structure and biodiversity). Biochar application to adjacent arable at 5-10 t/ha per 10-year cycle. Farm-scale Kon-Tiki or ring kiln most practical for strip-scale volumes.

registry.waterImpacts: Extreme Bio-Pumping: Rapid transpiration system designed to "drink" wet clays, while the harvested biochar acts as an ultimate flood-delay sponge when applied to soil.

registry.agronomicUtility: Biochar Soil Amendment: Application at 5-10 t/ha per decade improves soil water retention (+10-15% available water capacity), cation exchange capacity, and mycorrhizal activity. Biochar applied to this land must be kept out of any soil carbon sampling for land-stored carbon. Fuel savings from root-mediated compaction reduction. Carbon: any land-stored carbon claim would cover soil and roots only; harvested wood used for biochar is accounted under a biochar standard, never both. Viability requires minimum 6-year rotation and verified <20% MC at time of pyrolysis.

registry.soilTypeCondition: Upland brown earths and gleyed soils on hill farm boundaries. Land Classes 3–4.2. Avoid installation on peaty soils where pine establishment is unreliable.
registry.plantingRegime: 2 rows plus infill. Mix: 20% Sycamore, 20% Beech, 60% Scots Pine. Density: 2,500 SPH at 2m × 2m spacing. Plant as 1-year transplants. Nurse planting of faster-establishing Sycamore in outer row to protect slower-establishing Beech and Pine from early wind damage.
registry.maintenanceRegime: Year 1–3: Tree guards (1.2m heavy-duty mesh) essential for all stock. Spot weed around base of trees. Year 4–7: Formative pruning to develop clear, wind-firm single stems; remove co-dominant leaders. Year 8+: High-prune outer Sycamore rows to 2m clear stem to maintain understory airflow and prevent waterlogging. Long-term: No harvest (permanent windbreak function). Selective removal of dead or failing individuals only. No coppice rotation — the windbreak function requires permanent canopy.
registry.rootArchitecture: Sycamore: dense heart-root system 60–90cm depth; provides mid-soil structural stability and moderate hydraulic redistribution. Beech: wide-spreading lateral roots (0–50cm); binds headland soil; leaf litter creates deep forest floor organic layer for SOC accumulation. Austrian/Scots Pine: taproot to 1m+ in freely-draining sandy soils; excellent drought tolerance; root exudates improve mycorrhizal networks in adjacent arable soils.
registry.biodiversityImpacts: Specialist Invertebrate Habitat: Beech mast provides critical autumn food resource for Great Tit, Chaffinch, and Brambling. Pine needles and cones support specialist insect communities. Sycamore aphid colonies support a rich food web of natural enemy insects, bats, and small birds. Overall biodiversity is lower than native mixed woodland due to limited species diversity, but the dense structural complexity provides valuable nesting and foraging for common farmland birds.
registry.waterImpacts: Thermal Shelter and Microclimate: Reduces wind speed across a zone 10–20× canopy height, lowering evapotranspiration from adjacent crops. Reduces dew point stress and morning frost incidence on the lee side. Does not provide significant direct water quality benefit (no specialist N-fixing or P-trapping species). Indirect benefit: reduced soil erosion through lower wind-driven surface crust disruption.

Reduces crop lodging frequency by lowering peak gust speeds at ear height by 30–50% within 10× canopy height. Provides year-round livestock shelter (dairy heat stress reduction in summer via shade; lamb/calf protection in spring via wind reduction).

interventions.agronomicWindProfile: Maximum windbreak profile. Full 25m+ canopy height in Zone 2. Protection distance: 200-500m from woodland edge for crops in flat terrain.
